title: Apologia Pro Vita Sua
alternative_titles: Apologia Pro Vita Sua: Being a History of His Religious Opinions
description: Published in eight parts in 1864-65 in answer to Charles Kingsley's charge that he had taught that truth need not be kept with heretics: the greatest Victorian religious autobiography, and the book that restored Newman's reputation and made his name.
plot_or_argument: The Apologia narrates the development of Newman's religious opinions from his Evangelical childhood through the Oxford Movement, the Tracts for the Times, Tract 90, the move to Rome and the Oratory; the argument is that his changes were not inconsistencies but a coherent development under an authority he could not resist.
narrative_structure: The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
principal_characters: John Henry Newman; Charles Kingsley, his accuser; John Keble; Richard Hurrell Froude; Edward Pusey; Richard Whately
literary_form: Spiritual autobiography (in seven parts, with a supplementary chapter)
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the platform: the spoken sentence, the repetition and the triadic climax, the direct address to the audience, the apostrophe and the peroration, printed as delivered. The author's characteristic manner is ciceronian periods built on antithesis and climax.
historical_context: The 1864 controversy with Kingsley and the pages of Macmillan's and the Birmingham Oratory's pamphlet, the Oxford Movement's memory, and the position of Catholics in Victorian England after the restoration of the hierarchy in 1850.
literary_significance: The Apologia created the modern spiritual autobiography and is the most persuasive account in English of the grounds of religious belief; it is also the central historical document of the Oxford Movement, and its prose is the standard against which Victorian religious writing is measured.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Cardinal Newman. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Issued in weekly parts by Longman, Green from 23 May to 20 June 1864 and bound in June 1864; the book arose from Charles Kingsley's attack in Macmillan's Magazine and the correspondence that followed. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: The Idea of a University
alternative_titles: The Idea of a University Defined and Illustrated
description: The lectures delivered in Dublin in 1852 as rector of the new Catholic University, revised and collected with additional essays in 1873: the classic English defence of liberal education, and the source of the modern idea of the university.
plot_or_argument: Newman argues that knowledge is its own end, that the university is a place of teaching universal knowledge rather than of research or of professional training, that theology must be included among the sciences, and that the educated gentleman is the product of a liberal education; the later essays add the argument for the study of literature.
narrative_structure: The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
literary_form: Lectures and essays (Dublin, 1852; collected 1873 with the 1858 essays)
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the platform: the spoken sentence, the repetition and the triadic climax, the direct address to the audience, the apostrophe and the peroration, printed as delivered. The text is the printed lecture, retaining the spoken address. The author's characteristic manner is ciceronian periods built on antithesis and climax.
historical_context: The 1850s, the founding of the Catholic University of Ireland (1854) and the Oxford debates on the relation of university to Church, and the Victorian controversy over useful versus liberal knowledge (Huxley's 'Culture and Science' answered it in 1880).
literary_significance: The Idea of a University is the founding text of the modern debate on the purpose of higher education; its doctrine of knowledge as its own end and its portrait of the gentleman shaped the ideal of liberal education in England and America, and its argument against the purely utilitarian university is still the standard one used against vocational education.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Cardinal Newman. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Part I was published by John Henry Parker in 1852 as Discourses on the Scope and Nature of University Education; the expanded edition of 1858, published by Longman, Brown, carries the title The Idea of a University Defined and Illustrated. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Parochial and Plain Sermons
description: The sermons preached at St Mary's, Oxford, between 1828 and 1843 and published in eight volumes: the most influential body of Anglican preaching in the nineteenth century and the spiritual foundation of the Oxford Movement.
plot_or_argument: The sermons are single-argument meditations on the creed, the sacraments, sin, conscience and the unseen world, delivered to an academic congregation and designed to awaken a sense of the reality of God; the most famous, 'The Second Spring' (1852), belongs to the later Catholic collection.
narrative_structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the platform: the spoken sentence, the repetition and the triadic climax, the direct address to the audience, the apostrophe and the peroration, printed as delivered. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is ciceronian periods built on antithesis and climax.
historical_context: The 1830s at Oxford, the Noetics and the Oriel common room, the Evangelical revival and the High Church reaction that became the Oxford Movement. The record dates the work as composed between 1828 and 1843 and first published in 1834 and the corpus places it within Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement, it is catalogued under lecture and popular address; review essay and quarterly argument.
literary_significance: The Parochial and Plain Sermons created the devotional literature of the Oxford Movement and are the finest English sermons of the century: their doctrine of the 'invisible world' and their appeal to conscience shaped Victorian religious feeling and gave the Tractarians their popular voice.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Cardinal Newman. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1834, as collected sermons in eight volumes, by John Henry Newman. Composed between 1828 and 1843. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: The Dream of Gerontius
alternative_titles: The Dream of Gerontius: A Poem
description: Published in 1865 and set to music by Edward Elgar in 1900: a poem of the soul's journey after death, from the deathbed through judgment to purgatory, and one of the great Victorian poems on death. It is a verse work of 1865 by John Henry Newman; it belongs to Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement and it is catalogued here under Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence; Victorian Verse Drama and Revived Tragedy and the record grades it as major canon.
plot_or_argument: Gerontius dies, his soul is borne by the guardian angel through the regions of the air, hears the demons and the angelic choirs, is presented to God and, judged, passes to the cleansing fire of purgatory with the angel's song in his ears.
narrative_structure: An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.
principal_characters: Gerontius (the Soul); the Guardian Angel; the Priest and the assistants; the demons; the Angel of the Agony; the souls in Purgatory; the choirs of Angelicals
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse in the elegiac mode: the mourning stanzas run in a repeated stanzaic pattern, the line is long enough to carry the lament and the apostrophe, and the movement is from grief to the consolation or the refusal of consolation that closes the sequence. The author's characteristic manner is ciceronian periods built on antithesis and climax.
historical_context: The 1860s, the Catholic doctrine of purgatory, the Victorian literature of death and the deathbed, and Newman's own old age. The record dates the work as composed in 1865 and first published in 1865 and the corpus places it within Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement, it is catalogued under pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence; victorian verse drama and revived tragedy.
literary_significance: The Dream of Gerontius is the finest Victorian poem on death and the basis of Elgar's oratorio (1900), the greatest English choral work of the century; its imagery shaped the English imagination of the afterlife and its verse carries Newman's prose cadence into poetry.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Cardinal Newman. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Written in January and February 1865 and published in The Month for May and June 1865, and in the volume The Dream of Gerontius, The Martyr of Antioch, and Other Poems (Burns and Oates, October 1865). The record grades the work as major canon.

title: An Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine
alternative_titles: Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine
description: Published in 1845, in the months before Newman's reception into the Catholic Church: the argument that Catholic doctrine is the legitimate development of the original deposit of faith, and the theory that made his conversion intellectually possible.
plot_or_argument: Newman sets out the 'notes' of a true development — preservation of type, continuity of principles, power of assimilation, early anticipation, logical sequence, healing action, and chronic continuance — and tests the history of doctrine against them, concluding that the Roman Church is the legitimate heir of the early Church.
narrative_structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is ciceronian periods built on antithesis and climax.
historical_context: The 1840s, the Tract 90 controversy and the Anglican crisis, and the German and French controversies over doctrinal development (Möhler, Petavius). The record dates the work as composed between 1844 and 1845 and first published in 1845 and the corpus places it within Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.

title: The Christian Year: Thoughts in Verse for the Sundays and Holidays throughout the Year
alternative_titles: Christian Year: Thoughts in Verse for the Sundays and Holidays throughout the Year
description: Published anonymously in 1827 and the most widely read poetry book of the nineteenth century after the Bible and the hymnbook: a lyric for every Sunday and holy day of the Book of Common Prayer, written for family devotion.
plot_or_argument: Each poem takes the Gospel or Epistle of its day and turns it into a meditation — on the beauty of nature as a sign of grace, on childhood, on death, on the sacraments, and on the trusting submission of the soul to God; the sequence follows the liturgical year from Advent through Trinity and the saints' days.
narrative_structure: An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation. A sequence of sonnets, each complete in fourteen lines, reading as a continuous argument or a continuous story of feeling when taken in order.
literary_form: Poetry collection (109 poems, one for each Sunday and holy day)
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse in the elegiac mode: the mourning stanzas run in a repeated stanzaic pattern, the line is long enough to carry the lament and the apostrophe, and the movement is from grief to the consolation or the refusal of consolation that closes the sequence. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is simple, traditional metre and a limited imagery of nature and childhood.
historical_context: The 1820s-30s, the High Church devotional tradition, the Oxford of Oriel and the beginnings of the Oxford Movement, and the Victorian culture of family prayer. The record dates the work as composed between 1823 and 1825 and first published in 1827 and the corpus places it within Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement, it is catalogued under pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence; sonnet revival and sequenced sonnet.
literary_significance: The Christian Year was the most influential devotional poetry of the Victorian age and gave the Oxford Movement its popular voice; it shaped the spirituality of Newman and Pusey, and its Sunday-by-Sunday structure made it a permanent text of Anglican devotion and a model for later liturgical poetry.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1827, by John Keble. Composed between 1823 and 1825. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Lyra Apostolica
description: Published in the British Magazine in 1833-36 and as a collection in 1836, with contributions by Keble, Newman and Richard Hurrell Froude: the poetry of the Oxford Movement's first generation, and the verse that gave the Tractarians their militant and penitential tone.
plot_or_argument: The poems are short lyrics and sonnets on the Church, the sacraments, the power of the priesthood and the corruption of the age, many of them written on the Continental tour of Newman and Froude in 1832-33.
narrative_structure: A sequence of sonnets, each complete in fourteen lines, reading as a continuous argument or a continuous story of feeling when taken in order. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.
literary_form: Poetry collection (contributions with Newman and Froude)
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse in the fourteen-line sonnet, Petrarchan or Shakespearean, and in sequences where the individual sonnets accumulate into a continuous argument or a narrative of feeling. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is simple, traditional metre and a limited imagery of nature and childhood.
historical_context: The 1833 assize sermon and the founding of the Tracts, the Oxford Movement's early militancy, and the Romantic inheritance of Wordsworth and Scott in religious verse. The record dates the work as composed between 1833 and 1836 and first published in 1836 and the corpus places it within Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement, it is catalogued under sonnet revival and sequenced sonnet; pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence.
literary_significance: Lyra Apostolica is the primary poetic document of the Oxford Movement and the source of much of the devotional language of Victorian Anglo-Catholicism; its sonnets are among the earliest Victorian examples of the devotional sequence.
attribution_notes: The work is recorded as a joint undertaking with John Henry Newman and Richard Hurrell Froude, the contribution of each being stated in the work-author relationship. Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1836, as poetry collection (contributions with newman and froude), by John Keble. Composed between 1833 and 1836. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: The Rubáiyát of Omar Khayyám, the Astronomer-Poet of Persia
description: Published anonymously in 1859 in a paper wrapper at one shilling and largely ignored until Dante Gabriel Rossetti found it in 1861: the most famous English translation of Persian poetry and one of the most popular poems in the language.
plot_or_argument: The poem is a sequence of quatrains on the vanity of speculation and the urgency of present pleasure: the potter shapes the clay of dead men into pots; the Sultan and the Saint alike go down into dust; the only answer is wine and love 'here underneath the Bough, / A Jug of Wine, a Loaf of Bread — and Thou'.
narrative_structure: An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.
literary_form: Verse translation (75 quatrains in the first edition; 101 in the fourth, 1879)
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse in the elegiac mode: the mourning stanzas run in a repeated stanzaic pattern, the line is long enough to carry the lament and the apostrophe, and the movement is from grief to the consolation or the refusal of consolation that closes the sequence. The stanza is the quatrain. The author's characteristic manner is the Rubáiyát stanza (aaba, adapted from the Persian quatrain).
historical_context: The 1850s, the new English Orientalism and the study of Persian (Edward Cowell and the Bodleian manuscript), the Victorian crisis of faith, and the aesthetic movement's cult of melancholy pleasure. The record dates the work as composed between 1857 and 1859 and first published in 1859 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade; Arnold and the Criticism of Culture, it is catalogued under pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence; review essay and quarterly argument.
literary_significance: The Rubáiyát is the most popular English poem of the later nineteenth century and the founding text of the vogue for Persian literature; its celebration of the present moment and its scepticism made it the philosophical poem of the 1890s aesthetic movement, and its influence on the modern English quatrain and on the decoration (Rossetti, Morris, and the Kelmscott circle) is direct.
attribution_notes: A free adaptation rather than a literal translation: FitzGerald selected, rearranged and partly invented quatrains from the Persian and constructed a continuous poem. The first edition (1859) has 75 quatrains; the fourth (1879) has 101 and is the text usually reprinted.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1859, by Edward FitzGerald. Composed between 1857 and 1859. The title is also recorded as The Rubáiyát of Omar Khayyám. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: The Mighty Magician; or, The Two Ages of an Enchanter (after Calderón)
alternative_titles: The Mighty Magician; or, The Two Ages of an Enchanter
Mighty Magician; or, The Two Ages of an Enchanter (after Calderón)
description: FitzGerald's verse translation of Calderón's drama of the magician Cyprian and the martyr Justina, privately printed in 1853 and revised as The Mighty Magician (1865): one of the earliest English translations of Calderón and a key text of the Victorian revival of Spanish drama.
plot_or_argument: Cyprian, a pagan student, sells his soul to the devil for knowledge of Justina; he is converted by her faith and both die as martyrs, and the play enacts the triumph of grace over the magical will.
narrative_structure: A play in acts in blank verse, with the lyrical interludes and choruses set in shorter lines and in rhyme.
principal_characters: Cyprian; Justina; the Demon; Lelio and Floro
literary_form: Verse drama (translation of Calderón's El mágico prodigioso)
meter_and_prosody: Dramatic text. Verse drama in blank verse: the unrhymed iambic pentameter carries the dialogue, with lyrical interludes in shorter lines and in rhyme for songs, choruses and set pieces. The author's characteristic manner is the Rubáiyát stanza (aaba, adapted from the Persian quatrain).
historical_context: The 1840s-50s, the Victorian interest in Spanish drama (Lope de Vega, Calderón), and the Tractarian and Catholic revival of the period. The record dates the work as composed between 1850 and 1853 and first published in 1853 and it is catalogued under victorian verse drama and revived tragedy; dramatic monologue and masked lyric.
literary_significance: The Mighty Magician is the most important Victorian translation of Calderón and a significant document of the English revival of the Spanish Golden Age; its theme of the magician's bargain links it to Marlowe's Faustus, which FitzGerald and his circle saw as a native counterpart.

bibliographical_notes: First published in 1853, by Edward FitzGerald. Composed between 1850 and 1853. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Euphranor: A Dialogue on Youth
description: Published in 1851, a Socratic dialogue on education set in the Cambridge of the 1830s and modelled on Plato: a discussion of what a young man should be taught and how. It is a prose work of 1851 by Edward FitzGerald; it belongs to Arnold and the Criticism of Culture and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Lecture and Popular Address.
plot_or_argument: Euphranor and his friends debate the aims of education, the value of mathematics and the classics, the influence of the tutor and of the family, and the formation of character; the dialogue ends without a dogmatic conclusion.

The author's characteristic manner is the Rubáiyát stanza (aaba, adapted from the Persian quatrain).

The record dates the work as composed in None and first published in 1851 and the corpus places it within Arnold and the Criticism of Culture, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.

title: The English Constitution
description: First published as essays in the Fortnightly Review in 1865-66 and collected in 1867: the most influential work of English political science and the book that taught the world how the British constitution actually works.
plot_or_argument: Bagehot distinguishes the 'dignified' parts of the constitution — the monarchy and the House of Lords — whose function is to make government intelligible and acceptable to the people, from the 'efficient' parts — the cabinet, the House of Commons and the civil service — which actually govern; he then analyses the cabinet as a 'committee' of the legislature, the role of the Commons, the House of Lords, the monarchy and the change introduced by the Reform Act of 1867.
narrative_structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class.
historical_context: The 1860s, the Second Reform Act of 1867, the American Civil War and the comparison with the American presidency, and the new political journalism of the Fortnightly and the Economist. The record dates the work as composed between 1865 and 1867 and first published in 1867 and the corpus places it within Arnold and the Criticism of Culture, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
literary_significance: The English Constitution is the founding work of modern comparative political science: the 'dignified' and 'efficient' distinction is still the standard analysis of constitutional monarchy, and the book taught the nineteenth-century world how the British system worked. Its analysis of the cabinet and of the civil service shaped the study of government in Britain and the United States.

bibliographical_notes: First published in 1867, by Walter Bagehot. Composed between 1865 and 1867. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Physics and Politics; or, Thoughts on the Application of the Principles of 'Natural Selection' and 'Inheritance' to Political Society
description: Published in 1872 and first given as essays in the Fortnightly Review: the founding English work of social evolutionism, and an early attempt to apply Darwinian theory to the development of nations and to the question of why some societies progress and others do not.
plot_or_argument: Bagehot argues that progress depends on the 'cake of custom' being broken by a 'preliminary age of discussion', that the 'nation-making' period precedes the 'nation-keeping' one, and that the 'verifiable progress' of modern societies depends on the spread of the 'discussion' that only free institutions permit.
narrative_structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class.
historical_context: The 1860s-70s, the Darwinian revolution and the rise of social Darwinism, the unification of Germany and Italy, and the debate on the 'Aryan' and 'savage' races. The record dates the work as composed between 1867 and 1872 and first published in 1872 and the corpus places it within Arnold and the Criticism of Culture, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
literary_significance: Physics and Politics founded the evolutionary study of politics and introduced the idea of the 'age of discussion' as the mechanism of progress; it is a key text for the history of social Darwinism and for the modern critique of the Victorian idea of progress, and it influenced the sociology of Spencer, Maine and the American social scientists.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1872, as political and social theory (essays), by Walter Bagehot. Composed between 1867 and 1872. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Lombard Street: A Description of the Money Market
description: Published in 1873 and the classic English account of the money market: a description of how the Bank of England, the bill brokers and the joint-stock banks actually worked, and an argument for the Bank's responsibility as the holder of the ultimate reserve.
plot_or_argument: Bagehot describes the structure of the London money market, the role of the discount houses and the bill brokers, the 'one reserve' system of the Bank of England and the panic of 1866, and argues that in a crisis the Bank must lend freely at a high rate against good security — the 'lender of last resort' doctrine.
narrative_structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class.
historical_context: The 1866 collapse of Overend, Gurney and Co. and the panic that followed, the gold standard, and the Victorian debate on banking reform after the 1844 Act. The record dates the work as composed in 1872 and first published in 1873 and the corpus places it within Arnold and the Criticism of Culture, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
literary_significance: Lombard Street is the founding text of modern central banking: the 'lender of last resort' doctrine is still the basis of central bank behaviour in a crisis, and Bagehot's description of the money market is the classic account of how credit works. It shaped the Federal Reserve's response to the panics of the twentieth century and the 2008 crisis.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1873, as economic treatise, by Walter Bagehot. Composed in 1872. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: The English Constitution (Introduction to the Second Edition)
alternative_titles: English Constitution (Introduction to the Second Edition)
description: The long introduction added to the second edition of 1872, in which Bagehot revised his account of the constitution after the Reform Act of 1867 and the rise of the 'working man' as a political force.
plot_or_argument: Bagehot argues that the 1867 Act has made the House of Commons the real sovereign, that the 'theatrical' elements of the constitution have lost their hold on the new electorate, and that the 'efficient' parts must now be explained to a democratic public.
narrative_structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class.
historical_context: The 1867 Reform Act, the 1868 election and the first working-class MPs, and the debate on the future of the House of Lords. The record dates the work as composed in 1872 and first published in 1872 and the corpus places it within Arnold and the Criticism of Culture, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
literary_significance: The 1872 introduction is a foundational text for the study of the democratisation of British politics and the decline of the 'dignified' constitution; it is the classic statement of the shift from the mid-Victorian 'deferential' politics to the mass politics of the later century.

bibliographical_notes: First published in 1872, as political essay (preface), by Walter Bagehot. Composed in 1872. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Erewhon: or, Over the Range
description: Published anonymously in 1872 and one of the most original satires in English: the account of an imaginary country discovered beyond a mountain range, whose institutions invert those of Victorian England.
plot_or_argument: Higgs, a sheep farmer, crosses the range into Erewhon, where he finds a society in which sickness is a crime and crime is treated as illness, where the churches are 'Musical Banks', where 'hypothetical' language is forbidden, and where the 'Book of the Machines' records the debate on whether machines might become conscious and should be abolished. He falls in love with Arowhena and escapes with her in a balloon.
narrative_structure: A frame narrative in which the witness reports the machine, the society or the world, and the inventor explains his discovery in dialogue.
principal_characters: Higgs; Arowhena; Yram; Chowbok (Kahabuka); the Nosnibor family; the Professors
literary_form: Satirical utopian novel; early scientific romance
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the scientific romance: the frame narrative of the witness, the set-piece description of the machine, the society or the world, and the dialogue of exposition in which the inventor explains his discovery. The author's characteristic manner is swiftian inversion and the invented institution.
historical_context: The 1860s-70s, Darwinian theory, the machine age, the Victorian criminal law and the treatment of the insane, and Butler's own experience of New Zealand sheep farming. The record dates the work as composed in 1871 and first published in 1872 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under early scientific romance and utopian speculation; nonsense verse and the parody of rule.
literary_significance: Erewhon is the first English novel to treat the possibility of machine consciousness seriously (its 'Book of the Machines' anticipates the literature of artificial intelligence) and one of the sharpest satires on Victorian institutions; 'Erewhon' (nowhere) and 'Erewhonian' entered the language, and the book influenced Huxley, Orwell and the modern dystopia.

bibliographical_notes: First published in 1872, as satirical utopian novel, by Samuel Butler (1835-1902). Composed in 1871. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: The Way of All Flesh
description: Written between 1873 and 1884 and published posthumously in 1903: the most complete fictional indictment of the Victorian family, and the novel that made Butler a hero to the generation of Shaw and the Edwardian critics.
plot_or_argument: The novel follows four generations of the Pontifex family, from the tyrannical clergyman Theobald and his son Ernest, through Ernest's miserable childhood, his disastrous marriage to Ellen, his imprisonment for attempted assault, and his eventual inheritance and freedom, to the narrator Overton's amused commentary on the whole.
narrative_structure: A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
principal_characters: Ernest Pontifex; Theobald Pontifex; Christina Pontifex; George Pontifex; Alethea Pontifex; Overton; Ellen; Dr Skinner; Towneley
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The text was published posthumously, from the manuscript or from the papers left at the author's death. The author's characteristic manner is swiftian inversion and the invented institution.
historical_context: The 1830s-50s, the Victorian clergyman's household, the public school and the university, the law and the church as careers, and the social constraints on women and children. The record dates the work as composed between 1873 and 1884 and first published in 1903 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story; realist novel of common life.
literary_significance: The Way of All Flesh is the central English novel of Victorian family tyranny and one of the founding texts of the modern anti-Victorian reaction; its ironic narrator and its biological view of character influenced the Edwardian novel of the 'new woman' and the twentieth-century family novel, and it is the classic fictional statement of Butler's theory of hereditary habit.
attribution_notes: Published posthumously in 1903, nineteen years after it was written and the year after Butler's death; the text was prepared by R. A. Streatfeild, and Butler had left instructions that it should be published.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Richards in London in October 1903, a year after the author's death. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Life and Habit
description: Published in 1877, the first and most important of Butler's books against Darwin: an argument that heredity is a form of memory, that the embryo 'remembers' the habits of its ancestors, and that life is a series of unconscious recollections.
plot_or_argument: Butler argues that personal identity is continuous through the generations, that the development of the embryo is an act of memory, and that the 'variations' on which natural selection depends are themselves the result of effort and habit rather than random accident.
narrative_structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is swiftian inversion and the invented institution.
historical_context: The 1870s, the Darwinian controversy, the 'provisional' theory of pangenesis, and the debate on instinct and inheritance in the new biology. The record dates the work as composed between 1875 and 1877 and first published in 1877 and the corpus places it within Carlyle and the Hero-Worship Lecture; Arnold and the Criticism of Culture, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
literary_significance: Life and Habit is the founding text of the modern idea of the 'selfish gene' era's opposite — inherited memory and unconscious habit: Butler's theory influenced Bergson, the early twentieth-century biology of Hering and Semon, and the modern discussion of epigenetics and the inheritance of acquired characteristics. It is the central English contribution to the anti-Darwinian argument of the nineteenth century.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Samuel Butler. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Trübner in London in December 1877. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Erewhon Revisited Twenty Years Later, Both by the Original Discoverer of the Country and by His Son
description: Published in 1901, the year before Butler's death, and his own sequel to Erewhon: Higgs's own return, twenty years on, to the country where his escape by balloon has become a religion, told by his English son.
plot_or_argument: Higgs, the original discoverer, returns to Erewhon twenty years after his escape by balloon and finds that his ascent has become the basis of a new religion, 'Sunchildism', administered by the scheming Professors Hanky and Panky; he meets his Erewhonian son George, the child of Yram, his attempt to tell the truth is suppressed by the professors, and the story is told by his English son John.
narrative_structure: A frame narrative in which the witness reports the machine, the society or the world, and the inventor explains his discovery in dialogue.
principal_characters: Higgs, the original discoverer ('the Sunchild'); John Higgs, his English son and the narrator; George, his Erewhonian son; Yram, George's mother; Professors Hanky and Panky; Dr Downie
literary_form: Satirical utopian novel; early scientific romance
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the scientific romance: the frame narrative of the witness, the set-piece description of the machine, the society or the world, and the dialogue of exposition in which the inventor explains his discovery. The author's characteristic manner is swiftian inversion and the invented institution.
historical_context: The 1890s, the comparative study of religion and the 'higher criticism' of the Bible, the growth of the Victorian imperial cult, and Butler's interest in the 'historical Jesus' controversy. The record dates the work as composed between 1897 and 1901 and first published in 1901 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under early scientific romance and utopian speculation; nonsense verse and the parody of rule.
literary_significance: Erewhon Revisited is the classic English satire on the origin of religions and on the priestcraft that preserves them: it anticipates the modern sociology of religion and the fictional treatment of the historical Jesus, and its portrait of a belief system founded on a misunderstanding is among the most sophisticated in Victorian satire.

title: The Woman in White
alternative_titles: The Woman in White: A Novel
description: Serialised in Dickens's All the Year Round from November 1859 to August 1860 and published in three volumes: the first and greatest English sensation novel, and the book that made the phrase current. It is a prose fiction work of 1860 by Wilkie Collins; it belongs to Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot and it is catalogued here under Sensation Novel; Detective Story and the Tale of Detection and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: Walter Hartright, a drawing master, meets a woman dressed in white on the road to London and learns that she has escaped from an asylum; he goes to Limmeridge House to teach the half-sisters Laura Fairlie and Marian Halcombe, and Laura is married to Sir Percival Glyde, whose secret is an illegitimacy that invalidates his title. Glyde and Count Fosco confine Laura in the asylum in place of Anne Catherick, the woman in white, who has died; Marian and Walter recover Laura's identity through documents, and Glyde's secret is discovered and he dies in the burning church.
narrative_structure: Multiple first-person narration by the witnesses, assembled as evidence in a case. It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff.
principal_characters: Walter Hartright; Laura Fairlie; Marian Halcombe; Anne Catherick; Sir Percival Glyde; Count Fosco; Countess Fosco; Frederick Fairlie; Mr Gilmore; Mrs Catherick
literary_form: Sensation novel (All the Year Round, 1859-60; three volumes 1860)
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is documentary narration through letters, diaries and witness statements.
historical_context: The 1850s, the lunacy laws and the private asylum, the legal position of married women under coverture, the Matrimonial Causes Act of 1857, and the Italian political exiles in London. The record dates the work as composed between 1859 and 1860 and first published in 1860 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot, it is catalogued under sensation novel; detective story and the tale of detection.
literary_significance: The Woman in White is the defining sensation novel and one of the founding texts of the English detective story; its multiple narration, its critique of the legal non-existence of wives and its villain Count Fosco made it the model for the whole literature of mystery and testimony.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as William Wilkie Collins. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Serialised in All the Year Round from 29 November 1859 to 25 August 1860 and published in three volumes by Sampson Low in August 1860. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: The Moonstone
description: Serialised in All the Year Round in 1868 and described by T. S. Eliot as 'the first, the longest, and the best of modern English detective novels': the theft of a sacred Indian diamond from a Yorkshire country house, told by a succession of witnesses and solved by Sergeant Cuff.
plot_or_argument: The Moonstone, looted from a Hindu temple by a British officer, is left to his niece Rachel Verinder on her birthday and disappears that night; Sergeant Cuff's investigation, the suspicion of the servants, the devotion of the three Indian priests who follow the stone, and the discovery that Franklin Blake took it in an opium-induced trance lead through a London moneylender and a scientific experiment to the stone's return to India.
narrative_structure: Eight narratives by different witnesses, with a prologue at Seringapatam and an epilogue in India.
principal_characters: Sergeant Cuff; Franklin Blake; Rachel Verinder; Godfrey Ablewhite; Ezra Jennings; Gabriel Betteredge; Rosanna Spearman; Mr Bruff; Mr Murthwaite; Lady Verinder
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of detection: the pursuit narrative with the investigator's account of the evidence, the exact chronology and the reversal at the close. The author's characteristic manner is documentary narration through letters, diaries and witness statements.
historical_context: The 1860s, the empire and the colonial looting of India, the new detective police, the professionalisation of medicine, and the Victorian country house and its servants. The record dates the work as composed between 1867 and 1868 and first published in 1868 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot, it is catalogued under detective story and the tale of detection; sensation novel.
literary_significance: The Moonstone founded the English detective novel and established its conventions: the country-house crime, the closed circle of suspects, the professional detective, the chain of evidence and the final explanation. Its colonial subject makes it a central text of postcolonial criticism.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as William Wilkie Collins. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Serialised in All the Year Round from 4 January to 8 August 1868 and published in three volumes by Tinsley Brothers in July 1868. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: No Name
description: Serialised in All the Year Round in 1862: the story of Magdalen Vanstone, left illegitimate and penniless by the discovery that her parents' marriage was invalid, who sets out to recover her fortune by disguise and intrigue.
plot_or_argument: Magdalen and Norah Vanstone lose their name, inheritance and social position when their father's marriage is found void; Magdalen trains as an actress, adopts a series of disguises, pursues the heir Noel Vanstone and his housekeeper Mrs Lecount, marries him, and loses him to death and the will; the novel ends with her illness, her sister's marriage and her own quiet recovery.
narrative_structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff.
principal_characters: Magdalen Vanstone; Norah Vanstone; Captain Wragge; Noel Vanstone; Mrs Lecount; George Bartram; Admiral Bartram; Mr Pendril
literary_form: Sensation novel (All the Year Round, 1862; three volumes 1862)
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is documentary narration through letters, diaries and witness statements.
historical_context: The 1857 Matrimonial Causes Act and the law of legitimacy, the position of the illegitimate child, and the Victorian theatre. The record dates the work as composed in 1862 and first published in 1862 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot, it is catalogued under sensation novel; new woman and marriage-question novel.
literary_significance: No Name is the most direct Victorian novel about the legal construction of identity: Magdalen's loss of her name is a loss of her legal person, and the novel's argument for the reform of the law of legitimacy is as explicit as anything in the period.

title: Armadale
description: Serialised in the Cornhill Magazine from November 1864 to June 1866: the most complex of Collins's plots, built on a dream, a shipwreck and two generations of the Armadale name. It is a prose fiction work of 1866 by Wilkie Collins; it belongs to Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot and it is catalogued here under Sensation Novel; Ghost Story and Scientific Supernatural Tale and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: Allan Armadale is warned in a dream by a German doctor that he will meet a man who will be his fate and a woman who will be his ruin. He meets Ozias Midwinter, the son of the first Allan's victim, and Lydia Gwilt, a governess, forger and adventuress, who marries Midwinter in order to murder Armadale; the plot turns on a letter, a sanatorium and a poison, and ends with Lydia's death and Midwinter's survival.
narrative_structure: A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff. A short narrative in which the witness's account is given first, the strange event is approached by stages, and the explanation is withheld at the close.
principal_characters: Allan Armadale; Ozias Midwinter; Lydia Gwilt; Dr Downward; Mr Brock; Neelie Milroy; Mr Bashwood
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The author's characteristic manner is documentary narration through letters, diaries and witness statements.
historical_context: The 1860s, the law of the shipwreck and the insurance fraud, the private asylum, and the Victorian fascination with mesmerism and hereditary destiny. The record dates the work as composed between 1864 and 1866 and first published in 1866 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot, it is catalogued under sensation novel; ghost story and scientific supernatural tale.

bibliographical_notes: Serialised in The Cornhill Magazine from November 1864 to June 1866 and published in four volumes by Smith, Elder in June 1866. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: The Dead Secret
description: Serialised in Household Words in 1857 and the first of Collins's novels to show the full sensation method: a deathbed secret hidden in a Cornish house, and the slow uncovering of a substituted identity.
plot_or_argument: Mrs Treverton dictates on her deathbed a confession that Rosamond is not her daughter but the child of her maid, Sarah Leeson, passed off as her own to keep her husband's love; the confession is hidden in the Myrtle Room at Porthgenna Tower, and the novel follows the servant Sarah Leeson's flight, the search for the letter, and Rosamond's marriage and discovery of the truth.
narrative_structure: A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff. A short narrative in which the witness's account is given first, the strange event is approached by stages, and the explanation is withheld at the close.
principal_characters: Rosamond Frankland (née Treverton); Leonard Frankland, her blind husband; Sarah Leeson; Captain Treverton; Mrs Treverton; Uncle Joseph Buschmann; Andrew Treverton; Shrowl
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The author's characteristic manner is documentary narration through letters, diaries and witness statements.
historical_context: The 1850s, the Cornish setting and its wrecking economy, the Victorian deathbed and testament, and the Household Words readership. The record dates the work as composed between 1856 and 1857 and first published in 1857 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot, it is catalogued under sensation novel; ghost story and scientific supernatural tale.
literary_significance: The Dead Secret is the technical experiment in which Collins developed the method of The Woman in White — the hidden document, the withheld identity and the domestic secret.

title: The Haunted Hotel: A Mystery of Modern Venice
alternative_titles: Haunted Hotel: A Mystery of Modern Venice
description: Published in 1878 and the finest of Collins's shorter sensation works: the story of a Venetian palace, the disappearance of Lord Montbarry, and a dream that reveals a murder to a sleeping woman. It is a prose fiction work of 1878 by Wilkie Collins; it belongs to Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot and it is catalogued here under Ghost Story and Scientific Supernatural Tale; Detective Story and the Tale of Detection and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: Lord Montbarry abandons his fiancée Agnes for the Countess Narona and dies in Venice; the palace he bought becomes a hotel, and the guests are troubled by a smell, a stain and a dream. The Countess's confession reveals that Montbarry was murdered for his money, and the hotel's room yields the evidence.
narrative_structure: A short narrative in which the witness's account is given first, the strange event is approached by stages, and the explanation is withheld at the close. A narrative of pursuit and deduction, the evidence gathered in sequence and the reversal held for the close.
principal_characters: the Countess Narona; Lord Montbarry; Agnes Lockwood; Henry Westwick; Baron Rivar; Ferrari, the courier; Emily Ferrari; Dr Wybrow
literary_form: Novella; ghost story, first issued in 1878
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the supernatural: the rational first-person witness, the exact circumstantial detail that makes the impossible credible, the withheld explanation, and the closing sentence that leaves the reader with the horror unaccounted for. The author's characteristic manner is documentary narration through letters, diaries and witness statements.
historical_context: The 1870s, the Venetian tourist industry, and the Victorian interest in dreams and psychical research. The record dates the work as composed in 1878 and first published in 1878 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot, it is catalogued under ghost story and scientific supernatural tale; detective story and the tale of detection.
literary_significance: The Haunted Hotel is the most perfect of the English supernatural detective stories and a key text in the literature of the dream as evidence; it was a model for Henry James's later Venetian fiction.

title: The Law and the Lady
description: Published in 1875 and the first English detective novel with a woman as the investigator: Valeria Woodville's campaign to clear her husband of the murder of his first wife. It is a prose fiction work of 1875 by Wilkie Collins; it belongs to Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot and it is catalogued here under Detective Story and the Tale of Detection; New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: Valeria discovers on her honeymoon that her husband Eustace Macallan was tried for poisoning his first wife Sara, and that the Scottish verdict was 'not proven'. She investigates the case herself, travels to Scotland, interviews the witnesses, and establishes that Sara's death was suicide.
narrative_structure: A narrative of pursuit and deduction, the evidence gathered in sequence and the reversal held for the close. A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision.
principal_characters: Valeria Woodville (née Brinton), the narrator; Eustace Woodville (Eustace Macallan); Sara Macallan; Miserrimus Dexter; Ariel; Mrs Macallan, Eustace's mother; Major Fitz-David; Benjamin; Mr Playmore
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of detection: the pursuit narrative with the investigator's account of the evidence, the exact chronology and the reversal at the close. The author's characteristic manner is documentary narration through letters, diaries and witness statements.
historical_context: The 1870s, the Scottish verdict of 'not proven', the Victorian poison trials, and the position of a wife with no legal standing of her own. The record dates the work as composed between 1874 and 1875 and first published in 1875 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot; The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel, it is catalogued under detective story and the tale of detection; new woman and marriage-question novel.
literary_significance: The Law and the Lady is the founding English novel of the female detective: Valeria's investigation is an argument for a woman's intelligence and legal capacity, and the novel's use of the Scottish verdict made 'not proven' a permanent English phrase.
